terms.simpleDefinition: Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall after 20 weeks gestation.
terms.definition: An obstetric emergency presenting with painful dark vaginal bleeding, tense 'woody' tender uterus, uterine hypertonus, and acute foetal distress or demise.
terms.clinicalContext: NEVER perform digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded; establish two wide-bore 16G/18G IV lines, cross-match blood urgently, and prepare for emergency delivery.
terms.mnemonics: Abruption = Acute painful + Board-like uterus.

terms.simpleDefinition: The passage that allows air to move into and out of the lungs.
terms.definition: The airway includes the nose, mouth, throat, larynx, trachea and bronchi. A clear airway is essential for breathing.
terms.clinicalContext: Airway assessment is a first nursing priority. Obstruction, secretions, vomiting or reduced consciousness can quickly become life-threatening.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term airway when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: A medicine used to relieve pain.
terms.definition: Analgesics reduce pain through different mechanisms. Examples include paracetamol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines and opioids.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses assess pain before and after administration, check allergies, watch adverse effects and document response.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term analgesic when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Rapid, life-threatening systemic allergic reaction causing airway swelling and severe hypotension.
terms.definition: Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction triggering massive mast cell degranulation, bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, urticaria, and distributive shock.
terms.clinicalContext: IMMEDIATE FIRST-LINE: Adrenaline (Epinephrine) 1:1000 — 0.5 mg (0.5 mL) IM into anterolateral thigh (paediatric 0.01 mg/kg), lay patient flat with legs elevated, high-flow oxygen, and IV Normal Saline.
terms.mnemonics: ABCDE + Adrenaline IM Outer Thigh FIRST (never wait for antihistamine).

terms.simpleDefinition: A medicine used to treat bacterial infection.
terms.definition: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth. They do not treat viral infections unless bacterial infection is also present.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses check prescriptions, allergies, timing, route, cultures where ordered and patient response to treatment.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term antibiotic when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Standardized 0–10 newborn vitality score checked at 1 and 5 minutes after birth.
terms.definition: Evaluates Appearance (colour), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration — each scored 0, 1, or 2.
terms.clinicalContext: Never delay resuscitation to calculate the 1-minute Apgar score; begin drying, stimulation, and bag-valve-mask ventilation immediately if baby is apnoeic or gasping.
terms.mnemonics: A-P-G-A-R: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration (7–10 Normal).

terms.simpleDefinition: Abnormal accumulation of serous fluid within the peritoneal cavity.
terms.definition: Commonly caused by portal hypertension in liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, right heart failure, tuberculous peritonitis, or intra-abdominal malignancy.
terms.clinicalContext: Measure daily abdominal girth at the umbilicus and daily morning weight; monitor respiratory distress and electrolytes on spironolactone + furosemide or therapeutic paracentesis.

terms.simpleDefinition: Practices that prevent contamination by harmful microorganisms.
terms.definition: Asepsis means reducing or preventing the introduction of infection-causing organisms during care.
terms.clinicalContext: Hand hygiene, clean technique, sterile technique and safe handling of equipment protect patients from healthcare-associated infection.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term asepsis when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Entry of food, fluid, saliva or vomit into the airway.
terms.definition: Aspiration can irritate the lungs, block breathing or cause aspiration pneumonia.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses reduce risk by positioning patients safely, checking swallowing ability and monitoring coughing, choking or breathing changes.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term aspiration when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: The amount of sugar in the blood.
terms.definition: Blood glucose is a key energy measurement. It can become too high or too low in diabetes, illness, fasting or medication effects.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor glucose, recognize hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia signs and follow facility protocols.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term blood glucose when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: The force of blood pushing against artery walls.
terms.definition: Blood pressure is recorded as systolic pressure over diastolic pressure. It reflects circulation, vascular resistance and heart pumping action.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses measure blood pressure accurately, compare it with baseline and report very high, very low or rapidly changing readings.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term blood pressure when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Abnormally slow resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute in adults.
terms.definition: Can result from vagal stimulation, beta-blocker or digoxin toxicity, hypothyroidism, inferior MI, sick sinus syndrome, or increased intracranial pressure (Cushing's reflex).
terms.clinicalContext: Always hold digoxin or beta-blockers if adult HR < 60 bpm per facility protocol and assess blood pressure, dizziness, or syncope urgently.

terms.simpleDefinition: Medication that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle to open constricted airways.
terms.definition: Includes short-acting beta-2 agonists (Salbutamol), anticholinergics (Ipratropium), and methylxanthines (Aminophylline) used in asthma and COPD exacerbations.
terms.clinicalContext: Deliver short-acting Salbutamol FIRST before inhaled corticosteroids so bronchodilation opens airways cleanly; monitor heart rate for tachycardia and tremors.

terms.simpleDefinition: A quick test of blood flow to small vessels.
terms.definition: Capillary refill is checked by pressing a nail bed or skin area and observing how quickly normal colour returns.
terms.clinicalContext: Slow refill may suggest poor perfusion, cold exposure, dehydration or shock, and should be interpreted with other observations.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term capillary refill when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Critical drop in cardiac output caused by acute pump failure of the heart muscle.
terms.definition: Occurs after extensive myocardial infarction, myocarditis, or severe arrhythmias leading to hypotension (<90 mmHg SBP), cold clammy skin, oliguria, and pulmonary congestion.
terms.clinicalContext: Avoid rapid large IV fluid boluses unless preload-depleted because over-hydration worsens pulmonary oedema; monitor urine output hourly (<0.5 mL/kg/hr alert).

terms.simpleDefinition: The smallest living unit of the body.
terms.definition: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Cells use oxygen and nutrients, remove waste, respond to signals and reproduce when needed.
terms.clinicalContext: Poor oxygen, glucose or fluid balance affects cell function first, then tissues, organs and the whole patient.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term cell when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Bacterial infection of the foetal membranes (chorion and amnion) and amniotic fluid.
terms.definition: Presents during pregnancy or labour with maternal fever (>=38 C), maternal/foetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling amniotic fluid.
terms.clinicalContext: Limit unnecessary repeated vaginal exams after membrane rupture; start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per Uganda MoH guidelines and expedite safe delivery.

terms.simpleDefinition: Tissue that supports, binds, protects and connects body parts.
terms.definition: Connective tissue includes bone, cartilage, blood, adipose tissue and loose support tissue. It gives structure and support to organs and body systems.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses meet connective tissue concepts in wound healing, fractures, pressure injury prevention, blood disorders and mobility care.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term connective tissue when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Bluish discoloration of skin or mucous membranes from low oxygen.
terms.definition: Cyanosis is a clinical sign where the skin, lips or nail beds appear blue or dusky because blood oxygen is low.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses treat cyanosis as an urgent warning sign and assess airway, breathing, circulation and oxygen saturation.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term cyanosis when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Too little water in the body.
terms.definition: Dehydration occurs when fluid loss is greater than fluid intake. It may follow vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, bleeding, poor intake or excessive sweating.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses assess thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced urine, low blood pressure, fast pulse, poor skin turgor and altered consciousness.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term dehydration when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Loss of total body water and electrolytes exceeding intake, risking hypovolaemic shock in children.
terms.definition: WHO classifies paediatric diarrhoea into No Dehydration (Plan A: home ORS + Zinc), Some Dehydration (Plan B: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hrs), and Severe Dehydration (Plan C: IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg).
terms.clinicalContext: Assess sunken eyes, skin pinch elasticity, lethargy, and drinking ability; note Severe Acute Malnutrition children receive ReSoMal cautiously instead of rapid IV boluses.

terms.simpleDefinition: Life-threatening triad of hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, and ketonaemia in insulin deficiency.
terms.definition: Triggers osmotic diuresis, severe dehydration, Kussmaul deep rapid breathing, fruity acetone breath, abdominal pain, and potassium shifts.
terms.clinicalContext: Priority sequence: 1) IV 0.9% Normal Saline resuscitation FIRST, 2) Fixed-rate IV Soluble Insulin infusion, 3) Monitor serum K+ closely BEFORE and DURING insulin therapy to avoid fatal hypokalaemia.

terms.simpleDefinition: Subjective uncomfortable sensation of shortness of breath or laboured breathing.
terms.definition: Observed alongside nasal flaring, intercostal indrawing, tripod posturing, or accessory muscle usage across pneumonia, heart failure, asthma, and anaemia.
terms.clinicalContext: Place patient upright in High-Fowler's position, measure respiratory rate, auscultate lung fields, check SpO2, and escalate any drop <92%.

terms.simpleDefinition: New-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures or coma in a woman with pre-eclampsia.
terms.definition: Occurs antenatally, intrapartum, or up to 6 weeks postpartum due to severe cerebral vasospasm, endothelial dysfunction, and hypertensive encephalopathy.
terms.clinicalContext: Uganda MoH first-line drug of choice: Magnesium Sulphate (MgSO4 — 4 g IV loading + 10 g IM Pritchard regimen). Keep calcium gluconate 10% (1 g IV) at bedside and check RR >=16, urine output >=30 mL/hr, and patellar reflexes before every maintenance dose.
terms.mnemonics: 4g IV + 10g IM Pritchard -> Check Knees, Urine, Breaths!

terms.simpleDefinition: Swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues.
terms.definition: Edema is the accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces. It may occur in the legs, hands, face, abdomen or lungs.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses observe swelling, skin tightness, weight gain, shortness of breath and response to positioning or prescribed medicines.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term edema when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: A charged mineral in body fluids that supports nerves, muscles and fluid balance.
terms.definition: Electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride help regulate fluid movement, muscle contraction, heart rhythm and nerve function.
terms.clinicalContext: Abnormal electrolytes can cause weakness, confusion, seizures or dangerous heart rhythms, so nurses monitor results and report changes.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term electrolyte when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Sudden blockage of a pulmonary artery by a travelling blood clot, air bubble, or fat globule.
terms.definition: Usually originates from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in legs/pelvis, producing sudden pleuritic chest pain, acute dyspnoea, tachycardia, and haemoptysis.
terms.clinicalContext: Encourage early ambulation post-surgery and caesarean section; keep high-risk surgical/immobilized patients hydrated and administer prescribed LMWH prophylaxis.

terms.simpleDefinition: Microbial infection and vegetation growth on the inner lining and valves of the heart.
terms.definition: Complicates rheumatic heart disease, congenital valve defects, or unsterile IV access; causes prolonged fever, new regurgitant murmurs, splenomegaly, and embolic lesions.
terms.clinicalContext: Collect THREE sets of sterile blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites BEFORE starting IV antibiotics; strict aseptic IV line care is mandatory.

terms.simpleDefinition: Tissue that covers and protects surfaces inside and outside the body.
terms.definition: A type of tissue that covers body surfaces, lines internal cavities and forms glands. It acts as a protective barrier against infection, injury and fluid loss.
terms.clinicalContext: Damaged epithelial tissue increases infection risk. Nurses assess skin integrity, wound edges and mucous membranes during routine care.
terms.example: The lining of the mouth, the skin surface and the inner wall of the stomach are examples of epithelial tissue.
terms.mnemonics: Epithelial tissue covers, lines and forms glands.

terms.simpleDefinition: Seizure triggered by a rapid spike in fever in children typically aged 6 months to 5 years.
terms.definition: Simple febrile seizures are generalized, last under 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours; malaria, URTI, otitis media, or UTI are common triggers in Uganda.
terms.clinicalContext: Protect head, turn child to left-lateral recovery position, do NOT force anything into the mouth, give rectal Diazepam 0.5 mg/kg if >5 minutes, and evaluate urgently to rule out meningitis and severe malaria.

terms.simpleDefinition: A body temperature higher than normal.
terms.definition: Fever is often a response to infection, inflammation or other illness. It reflects changes in temperature regulation.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor temperature trends, hydration, comfort, prescribed medicines and danger signs such as confusion or stiff neck.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term fever when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Abnormal opening between bladder and vagina caused by prolonged obstructed labour.
terms.definition: Ischaemic necrosis from sustained foetal head compression destroys pelvic tissues, resulting in continuous uncontrollable leakage of urine per vaginum and skin excoriation.
terms.clinicalContext: Prevention via early partograph monitoring and timely Caesarean section; post-repair nursing demands continuous bladder drainage (Foley catheter strictly patent for 14–21 days) and strict fluid intake >=3 L/day.

terms.simpleDefinition: Standardized 3–15 point neurological scale assessing Eye opening, Verbal response, and Motor response.
terms.definition: Scores Eye (1–4), Verbal (1–5), and Motor (1–6). GCS <=8 indicates severe coma and inability to protect the airway.
terms.clinicalContext: 'GCS 8 or less — Intubate / Secure Airway!' Always record component breakdown (e.g., E3 V4 M6 = 13/15) rather than only a total sum, and escalate any drop >=2 points immediately.
terms.mnemonics: Eyes 4, Verbal 5, Motor 6 = 15 max (8 or less = Coma).

terms.simpleDefinition: Presence of measurable glucose in urine when blood sugar exceeds renal threshold (~10 mmol/L).
terms.definition: Detected cleanly via urine reagent dipstick strips; hallmark screening finding in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, gestational diabetes, or renal tubular dysfunction.
terms.clinicalContext: Any positive urine glucose must be followed with capillary random/fasting blood glucose testing and dipstick ketones check.

terms.simpleDefinition: Obstetric shorthand recording total pregnancies (Gravida) and viable births >=28 weeks (Parity).
terms.definition: In Uganda's obstetric practice, viability is conventionally counted from 28 weeks gestation (or >1000 g); e.g., G3P2+0 means 3 pregnancies, 2 deliveries >=28 wks, 0 abortions/losses.
terms.clinicalContext: Grand multiparity (>=5 deliveries) carries elevated risk of uterine atony, malpresentation, and postpartum haemorrhage—actively prepare AMTSL and uterotonics.

terms.simpleDefinition: Coughing up blood or blood-stained sputum from the lower respiratory tract.
terms.definition: Key red-flag symptom in Pulmonary Tuberculosis (PTB), bronchiectasis, lung abscess, pulmonary embolism, or mitral stenosis; distinct from haematemesis (vomited GI blood).
terms.clinicalContext: Initiate airborne/droplet respiratory isolation precautions immediately if chronic cough >2 weeks + weight loss/night sweats is present, and send sputum GeneXpert / AFB.

terms.simpleDefinition: Blood loss >=500 mL after vaginal delivery or >=1000 mL after Caesarean section.
terms.definition: Leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide; driven by the '4 Ts': Tone (uterine atony ~70%), Trauma (cervical/vaginal tears), Tissue (retained placenta), and Thrombin (coagulopathy).
terms.clinicalContext: Act immediately: Call for help, bimanual/fundal uterine massage, Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV + 20–40 IU infusion, empty bladder, inspect tears, give Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours.
terms.mnemonics: 4 Ts of PPH: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin.

terms.simpleDefinition: Bleeding from a damaged blood vessel.
terms.definition: Hemorrhage may be external or internal and can lead to shock if blood loss is significant.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor bleeding, pulse, blood pressure, skin condition, consciousness and urine output while escalating urgently.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term hemorrhage when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: The body's ability to keep internal conditions stable.
terms.definition: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes inside or outside the body.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses support homeostasis through monitoring vital signs, fluids, glucose, temperature, oxygenation and elimination.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term homeostasis when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Dangerously elevated serum potassium above 5.5 mmol/L risking fatal cardiac arrest.
terms.definition: Common in acute kidney injury (AKI), severe burns/crush trauma, DKA before therapy, or ACE-inhibitor overuse; ECG shows tall peaked T-waves and widened QRS.
terms.clinicalContext: Immediate cardiac membrane protection uses IV Calcium Gluconate 10% (10 mL slow IV over 3–5 min), followed by Insulin-Dextrose infusion to shift K+ intracellularly.

terms.simpleDefinition: Blood pressure that remains higher than normal.
terms.definition: Hypertension increases strain on the heart and blood vessels and raises the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney disease.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses measure accurately, support lifestyle education, monitor medicine adherence and report very high readings or symptoms.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term hypertension when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Dangerously low blood glucose (<3.9 mmol/L in diabetics, <2.5 mmol/L in severe malaria/paediatrics).
terms.definition: Triggers autonomic signs (sweating, palpitations, tremor, hunger) progressing swiftly to neuroglycopenia (confusion, convulsions, coma) especially with Quinine/Artesunate or Insulin therapy.
terms.clinicalContext: Check capillary blood glucose in EVERY confused or convulsing patient immediately. Give 50% Dextrose 50 mL IV in adults (or 10% Dextrose 2–5 mL/kg IV in children) if unconscious.
terms.mnemonics: Cold & clammy -> Give sugar candy (Oral 15g) or IV Dextrose if drowsy!

terms.simpleDefinition: Acute inadequate organ perfusion from rapid loss of circulating blood or plasma volume.
terms.definition: Triggered by trauma bleeding, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, PPH, burns, or cholera diarrhoea; shows tachycardia FIRST before late blood pressure drop, capillary refill >3 s, and oliguria.
terms.clinicalContext: Tachycardia and cool extremities appear BEFORE hypotension; insert two large-bore 16G/18G cannulae, raise legs, infuse warm Ringer's Lactate or cross-matched blood.

terms.simpleDefinition: Not enough oxygen reaching body tissues.
terms.definition: Hypoxia occurs when tissues receive insufficient oxygen for normal function. It may result from airway obstruction, lung disease, poor circulation or anaemia.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, mental status, cyanosis and work of breathing, then escalate quickly when oxygenation is unsafe.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term hypoxia when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Yellowish staining of the sclerae (whites of the eyes) and mucous membranes due to hyperbilirubinaemia.
terms.definition: Typically becomes clinically detectable in sclerae when total serum bilirubin exceeds ~35–50 micromol/L in hepatitis, malaria haemolysis, or biliary obstruction.
terms.clinicalContext: Always inspect sclerae in natural daylight rather than dim yellow ward bulbs; pair with checking urine colour (dark tea-like) and stool colour (pale/clay in obstruction).

terms.simpleDefinition: Invasion and multiplication of harmful microorganisms in the body.
terms.definition: Infection occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites enter and multiply, causing local or systemic effects.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor temperature, pain, swelling, wound discharge, respiratory symptoms and sepsis warning signs.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term infection when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: The body's protective response to injury or infection.
terms.definition: Inflammation is a response involving redness, heat, swelling, pain and sometimes loss of function.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses observe inflammatory signs around wounds, cannula sites, joints and mucous membranes, then document and report concerns.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term inflammation when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: An injection given into muscle.
terms.definition: An intramuscular injection places medicine into muscle tissue for absorption into the bloodstream.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses select the correct site, needle size, angle and infection prevention steps while observing for pain or reaction.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term intramuscular injection when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Given into a vein.
terms.definition: Intravenous, often shortened to IV, means a medicine or fluid is delivered directly into the venous circulation.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor cannula site, fluid rate, compatibility, infiltration, phlebitis and patient response.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term intravenous when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Telescoping of one proximal segment of bowel inside an adjacent distal segment causing obstruction.
terms.definition: Classic paediatric surgical emergency (ages 3–24 months) presenting with intermittent severe colicky crying, drawing knees up, vomiting, 'red currant jelly' mucoid bloody stool, and sausage-shaped RUQ mass.
terms.clinicalContext: Keep strictly Nil By Mouth (NBM), insert NG decompression tube, hydrate IV, and refer immediately to surgical theatre for hydrostatic reduction or laparotomy.

terms.simpleDefinition: Yellow skin and eye discolouration in newborns from elevated unconjugated or conjugated bilirubin.
terms.definition: Physiological jaundice starts AFTER 24 hours of life; jaundice appearing within the FIRST 24 HOURS is ALWAYS pathological (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD, sepsis) and risks kernicterus brain damage.
terms.clinicalContext: Any jaundice within 24 hours of birth or reaching palms/soles is an EMERGENCY requiring serum bilirubin check and immediate phototherapy with eye shields + extra hydration.

terms.simpleDefinition: Clinical bedside estimate of right atrial pressure observed via internal jugular vein pulsations.
terms.definition: Measured with patient resting comfortably at 45 degrees elevation; normal vertical height is <=3–4 cm above the sternal angle of Louis.
terms.clinicalContext: Elevated JVP flags right-sided heart failure, fluid overload during IV therapy, tension pneumothorax, or cardiac tamponade—slow IV fluids immediately and notify clinician.

terms.simpleDefinition: Irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy causing permanent brain injury in severely jaundiced newborns.
terms.definition: Unconjugated lipid-soluble bilirubin crosses the immature neonatal blood-brain barrier and deposits in basal ganglia, producing high-pitched cry, opisthotonus (arched back), hypotonia, and deafness/cerebral palsy.
terms.clinicalContext: Preventable through early phototherapy screening and exchange blood transfusion thresholds; monitor poor feeding and lethargy in all jaundiced neonates.

terms.simpleDefinition: Tiny bluish-white grain-of-salt lesions on bright red buccal mucosa — pathognomonic of Measles.
terms.definition: Appear inside the mouth opposite the upper molar teeth 1–2 days BEFORE the generalized maculopapular measles rash erupts alongside coryza, cough, and conjunctivitis.
terms.clinicalContext: Early recognition triggers strict airborne isolation, Vitamin A supplementation (2 doses per Uganda MoH), and public health surveillance reporting.

terms.simpleDefinition: Deep, rapid, sighing hyperventilation attempting to blow off CO2 in severe metabolic acidosis.
terms.definition: Classic compensatory respiratory drive seen in Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), renal failure uraemia, severe sepsis lactic acidosis, and salicylate poisoning.
terms.clinicalContext: Never treat Kussmaul breathing as primary respiratory failure requiring sedation—correct the underlying metabolic acidosis (IV fluids/insulin).

terms.simpleDefinition: Normal postpartum uterine discharge flowing for 4–6 weeks after childbirth.
terms.definition: Progresses sequentially: Lochia Rubra (bright red days 1–4), Lochia Serosa (pinkish-brown days 5–10), and Lochia Alba (yellowish-white days 11–28).
terms.clinicalContext: Foul-smelling lochia, sudden return to heavy bright bleeding, large clots, or sub-involution with fever signals puerperal sepsis or retained placental fragments.

terms.simpleDefinition: Sterile needle insertion into the lumbar subarachnoid space (L3–L4 or L4–L5) to sample CSF.
terms.definition: Diagnoses bacterial/cryptococcal meningitis, encephalitis, and subarachnoid haemorrhage using opening pressure, cell counts, protein, glucose, and India Ink/CrAg/culture.
terms.clinicalContext: Position patient curled tightly in fetal lateral or sitting posture; monitor for post-LP headache, CSF leak, or lower-limb tingling, and never perform if focal neuro signs/papilloedema indicate herniation risk.

terms.simpleDefinition: General feeling of bodily discomfort, fatigue, and lack of well-being marking infection onset.
terms.definition: Early non-specific prodromal symptom of acute viral infections, malaria, HIV seroconversion, tuberculosis, and autoimmune flares.
terms.clinicalContext: Probe onset timeline, rigors, weight change, and localizing organ symptoms during holistic nursing history.

terms.simpleDefinition: Dark greenish-black tarry first newborn stool formed from ingested amniotic debris in utero.
terms.definition: Passage within 24–48 hours confirms lower GI patency; fresh thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid during cephalic labour signals foetal distress and aspiration risk.
terms.clinicalContext: Delayed meconium >48 hrs suggests Hirschsprung disease or imperforate anus; for vigorous babies born through meconium, dry/stimulate without routine deep tracheal suction.

terms.simpleDefinition: Black, tarry, foul-smelling stools caused by digested blood from upper GI bleeding.
terms.definition: Stomach acid digests haemoglobin from bleeding peptic ulcers, oesophageal varices, or NSAID gastritis into dark tarry stools (>50 mL blood loss needed).
terms.clinicalContext: Distinguish true melaena from dark stools caused by oral iron tablets (non-foul); monitor pulse, BP, postural drop, haemoglobin, and cross-match urgently.

terms.simpleDefinition: All the chemical reactions that keep the body alive.
terms.definition: Metabolism includes reactions that build body materials and reactions that break down nutrients to release energy.
terms.clinicalContext: Changes in metabolism may appear as altered temperature, weight change, fatigue, glucose imbalance or poor wound healing.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term metabolism when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Tissue that contracts to produce movement.
terms.definition: Muscle tissue is specialized for contraction. Skeletal muscle moves the body, cardiac muscle pumps blood and smooth muscle moves substances through organs.
terms.clinicalContext: Weakness, cramps, paralysis and reduced mobility can reflect muscle or nerve problems that require careful nursing assessment.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term muscle tissue when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: A heart attack caused by blocked blood supply to heart muscle.
terms.definition: Myocardial infarction occurs when part of the heart muscle is injured because oxygen-rich blood cannot reach it.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses treat chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, nausea or collapse as urgent, monitor vital signs and support emergency care.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term myocardial infarction when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Kidney glomerular disorder causing heavy proteinuria, low blood albumin, generalized oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
terms.definition: Damaged glomerular basement membrane leaks >3.5 g protein daily, slashing oncotic pressure and creating periorbital/pedal oedema, ascites, and infection susceptibility.
terms.clinicalContext: Track strict daily weights, fluid intake/output chart, urine dipstick protein, abdominal girth, and protect fragile oedematous skin from breakdown.

terms.simpleDefinition: Tissue that receives and sends messages in the body.
terms.definition: Nervous tissue is made of neurons and support cells. It detects change, carries impulses and coordinates body responses.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses assess consciousness, orientation, pain response, pupil reaction and limb movement to monitor nervous system function.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term nervous tissue when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Abnormally low urine output (<400 mL/24 hrs or <0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults); anuria is <100 mL/24 hrs.
terms.definition: Critical early marker of pre-renal hypovolaemia/shock, intrinsic acute kidney injury (nephrotoxins, blackwater fever), or post-renal Foley catheter/prostatic obstruction.
terms.clinicalContext: Before assuming kidney failure in catheterized patients, FIRST flush/inspect Foley tubing for kinks or clots! Monitor MgSO4 patients closely—withhold MgSO4 if urine <30 mL/hr.

terms.simpleDefinition: A body structure made from two or more tissues with a specific job.
terms.definition: An organ is formed when tissues work together for a specific function. Examples include the heart, lungs, kidneys, skin, stomach and brain.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses assess organ function by observing breathing, pulse, urine output, skin condition, consciousness and other clinical signs.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term organ when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: A group of organs working together for a major body function.
terms.definition: An organ system is a set of organs that cooperate to maintain life, such as the respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive and urinary systems.
terms.clinicalContext: System thinking helps nurses prioritize airway, breathing, circulation, elimination, nutrition and neurological status.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term organ system when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Shortness of breath triggered when lying flat that relieves when propped upright on pillows.
terms.definition: Classic hallmark of left ventricular congestive heart failure as supine posture shifts peripheral venous blood centrally into congested pulmonary capillaries.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurse patient comfortably upright (45–90 degrees Fowler's) supported on pillows or cardiac table; record '2-pillow' or '3-pillow orthopnoea' baseline.

terms.simpleDefinition: The percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen in the blood.
terms.definition: Oxygen saturation is commonly measured with a pulse oximeter and helps estimate how well oxygen is being carried.
terms.clinicalContext: A falling saturation can be an early danger sign. Nurses confirm probe placement, assess the patient and escalate according to protocol.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term oxygen saturation when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: WHO graphical labour chart tracking cervical dilatation, contractions, and maternal-foetal status.
terms.definition: Begins plotting strictly once active first-stage labour reaches >=4 cm cervical dilatation; compares dilatation pace against the Alert Line (1 cm/hr) and Action Line (+4 hrs).
terms.clinicalContext: Crossing the Alert Line warrants heightened monitoring/referral readiness; reaching the Action Line triggers urgent obstetric intervention for prolonged/obstructed labour.

terms.simpleDefinition: Pregnancy-specific disorder after 20 weeks marked by new hypertension (>=140/90 mmHg) and proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
terms.definition: Driven by abnormal placental spiral artery remodelling causing vasospasm, endothelial leak, oedema, hyperreflexia, epigastric RUQ pain, and thrombocytopenia (HELLP).
terms.clinicalContext: Screen every ANC mother cleanly with calibrated BP cuff + urine protein dipstick; treat severe BP >=160/110 promptly with Nifedipine or IV Hydralazine + MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis.

terms.simpleDefinition: Severe bacterial genital tract infection occurring from membrane rupture/delivery up to 42 days postpartum.
terms.definition: Defined clinically by fever >=38 C with pelvic pain, foul lochia, sub-involution of uterus, tachycardia, and tachypnoea; commonly polymicrobial (Streptococci, E. coli, anaerobes).
terms.clinicalContext: Prevention via strict 5-Cleans delivery asepsis; treat early with Triple IV Antibiotics (Ampicillin + Gentamicin + Metronidazole) per Uganda Clinical Guidelines.

terms.simpleDefinition: The beat felt as blood is pumped through arteries.
terms.definition: Pulse is the rhythmic expansion of an artery caused by heart contraction. It is assessed by rate, rhythm, strength and equality.
terms.clinicalContext: Pulse assessment helps nurses identify pain, fever, dehydration, shock, arrhythmia and response to treatment.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term pulse when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Sharp ECG waveform deflection representing rapid ventricular depolarization (contraction).
terms.definition: Normal QRS duration is <0.12 seconds (<3 small ECG squares). Widened QRS suggests ventricular tachycardia, bundle branch block, or severe hyperkalaemia.
terms.clinicalContext: In cardiac arrest strips, rapid broad-complex rhythm without pulse = pulseless VT requiring immediate defibrillation.

terms.simpleDefinition: First fluttering sensations of foetal movement felt by the mother, usually between 16–20 weeks.
terms.definition: Reassuring maternal milestone confirming foetal neuromuscular vitality; multigravidas typically perceive quickening ~2 weeks earlier than primigravidas.
terms.clinicalContext: After 28 weeks, instruct mothers to count '10 kicks within 2 hours' or monitor daily foetal movements and report any marked reduction urgently.

terms.simpleDefinition: The act of breathing in oxygen and breathing out carbon dioxide.
terms.definition: Respiration includes ventilation and gas exchange. Nurses assess rate, depth, rhythm, effort and breath sounds.
terms.clinicalContext: Abnormal respiration may indicate pain, anxiety, infection, asthma, hypoxia, shock or neurological changes.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term respiration when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Maternal antibody development against Rh-positive foetal red cells risking haemolytic disease of newborn.
terms.definition: Occurs when an RhD-negative mother is exposed to RhD-positive foetal blood during birth, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or trauma without Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis.
terms.clinicalContext: Check maternal ABO/Rh blood group at first ANC booking! Administer Anti-D immunoglobulin IM within 72 hours of delivery, abortion, or sensitizing bleed if baby is Rh+.

terms.simpleDefinition: Violent uncontrollable shivering chills accompanied by teeth chattering as core fever rises steeply.
terms.definition: Classic hallmark of sudden pyrogen surges in acute malaria paroxysms, septicaemia, pyelonephritis, pneumonia, or acute blood transfusion reactions.
terms.clinicalContext: Obtain blood smear/RDT for malaria + blood cultures BEFORE empirical antipyretics when safe; remove heavy blankets only once shivering stops and hot phase begins.

terms.simpleDefinition: A life-threatening body response to infection.
terms.definition: Sepsis is severe organ-threatening illness caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses monitor temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, mental status and urine output, then escalate immediately when sepsis is suspected.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term sepsis when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: A life-threatening state where tissues do not receive enough blood flow and oxygen.
terms.definition: Shock occurs when circulation cannot meet tissue needs. Causes include blood loss, severe infection, heart problems and allergic reactions.
terms.clinicalContext: Nursing priorities include rapid recognition, airway and breathing support, circulation monitoring, fluid preparation and urgent escalation.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term shock when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: High-pitched harsh crowing sound predominantly on INSPIRATION indicating upper airway narrowing.
terms.definition: Signifies acute partial obstruction at larynx or trachea from croup, epiglottitis, anaphylaxis angioedema, inhaled foreign body, or post-extubation oedema.
terms.clinicalContext: EMERGENCY RED FLAG: Stridor at rest demands calm positioning (on caregiver's lap), humidified oxygen, nebulized Adrenaline + Dexamethasone, and NEVER agitate the child with throat spatulas!

terms.simpleDefinition: Sudden brain injury caused by blocked or bleeding blood vessels.
terms.definition: Stroke occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted or bleeding occurs in the brain.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses watch for facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty, altered consciousness and urgent onset time documentation.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term stroke when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: An injection given into the fatty layer under the skin.
terms.definition: A subcutaneous injection places medicine into tissue below the skin and above the muscle.
terms.clinicalContext: Common examples include insulin and some anticoagulants. Nurses rotate sites and assess for bruising or irritation.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term subcutaneous injection when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Abnormally rapid breathing rate exceeding normal age thresholds.
terms.definition: WHO pneumonia fast-breathing cut-offs: >=60/min (age <2 months), >=50/min (2–11 months), >=40/min (1–5 years), and >20/min in resting adults.
terms.clinicalContext: Count full 60 seconds when child is calm; tachypnoea is the single most sensitive early sign of childhood pneumonia before crackles appear!

terms.simpleDefinition: A measurement of body heat.
terms.definition: Body temperature shows the balance between heat production and heat loss. Fever or low temperature can signal illness or environmental stress.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses record temperature, compare trends and link findings to infection, dehydration, exposure or medication effects.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term temperature when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: A group of similar cells working together for one function.
terms.definition: A tissue is a level of body organization between cells and organs. The four major tissue groups are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue.
terms.clinicalContext: Understanding tissue helps nurses connect wounds, inflammation, oxygen supply and healing to the patient's overall condition.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term tissue when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Failure of uterine myometrial muscles to contract firmly after childbirth, leaving a soft boggy uterus.
terms.definition: Permits rapid torrential bleeding from open placental-site spiral arteries; accounts for ~70% of primary postpartum haemorrhage cases.
terms.clinicalContext: Prevent routinely with Active Management of Third Stage of Labour (Oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 minute of birth); feel abdomen immediately postpartum—boggy = massage + uterotonics!

terms.simpleDefinition: Severe ischaemic pain crisis when sickled red blood cells block small capillaries in bones or organs.
terms.definition: Triggered in Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS) by dehydration, hypoxia, cold weather, or infections (malaria/pneumonia), presenting as dactylitis, long bone pain, or acute chest syndrome.
terms.clinicalContext: Priority triage triad: 1) Rapid IV/oral Hydration, 2) Adequate stepped Analgesia (Paracetamol + Ibuprofen/Morphine—never delay opioids!), 3) Oxygen + keep warm + treat infection.

terms.simpleDefinition: Continuous high-pitched musical whistling sounds predominantly on EXPIRATION from narrowed small airways.
terms.definition: Indicates bronchospasm, airway oedema, or mucus plugging in bronchial asthma, infant bronchiolitis, COPD, or anaphylaxis.
terms.clinicalContext: A sudden 'SILENT CHEST' with poor air entry in severe asthma means extreme danger (exhaustion/imminent arrest), NOT improvement!

terms.simpleDefinition: A break or injury in body tissue.
terms.definition: A wound may involve skin, mucous membrane or deeper tissue. It can result from surgery, trauma, pressure, burns or disease.
terms.clinicalContext: Nurses assess wound size, depth, edges, exudate, odour, pain, surrounding skin and signs of infection.
terms.example: In practice, nurses use the term wound when assessing, documenting or explaining patient care.
terms.mnemonics: Connect the word to assessment, documentation and safe nursing action.

terms.simpleDefinition: Partial or complete separation/bursting open of previously sutured surgical wound edges.
terms.definition: Often heralded on postoperative days 5–8 by sudden gush of serosanguinous ('pink watery') fluid; if viscera protrude through fascia, it is called EVISCERATION.
terms.clinicalContext: In Evisceration: STAY CALM, call surgeon stat, do NOT push organs back in—cover viscera with sterile saline-soaked gauze, bend patient's knees slightly (low-Fowler's), keep NBM.

terms.simpleDefinition: Common radiographic imaging assessing lungs, heart silhouette, ribs, pneumothorax, and ETT/NGT positions.
terms.definition: Reveals lobar consolidation, pleural effusion meniscus, tension pneumothorax tracheal shift, cardiomegaly, and tuberculosis apical cavities.
terms.clinicalContext: Always verify pregnancy status BEFORE abdominal/pelvic X-rays in reproductive-age women and apply lead shielding when clinically feasible.

terms.simpleDefinition: Acute viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted by daytime-biting Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
terms.definition: Features acute fever, severe backache, bradycardia-fever dissociation (Faget's sign), progressing in severe toxic phase to jaundice, haematemesis ('black vomit'), and renal failure.
terms.clinicalContext: Single lifetime Yellow Fever vaccine (Stamaril) confers lifelong immunity at >=99%; immediate notifiable viral haemorrhagic surveillance alert in Uganda.

terms.simpleDefinition: Essential WHO adjunct therapy given alongside ORS for acute childhood diarrhoea.
terms.definition: Dispersible Zinc sulphate (20 mg once daily for 10–14 days in children >=6 months; 10 mg if <6 months) restores intestinal mucosal brush border and reduces episode severity/recurrence.
terms.clinicalContext: Give strictly WITH ORS (never as a standalone replacement for fluids!) and advise mothers to finish the full 10-day course even after diarrhoea stops.
